A penny is the name of the smallest coin in a currency system — the coin with the least value. Think of it as the lowest rung on the ladder of money.
Penny in the United States and Canada

In the US and Canada, a penny is a coin worth one cent, which means it takes 100 pennies to make one dollar. It is the coin you'd receive as change when, for example, something costs $0.99 and you pay $1.00 — the single coin you get back is a penny.

In the US, the penny features the face of Abraham Lincoln on one side. It is typically copper-colored and is the coin most people consider barely worth picking up off the ground — which itself tells you something about how little it is worth in modern life.

In British English, the word "penny" has two related but slightly different jobs, and this is where things get a little interesting.

One penny = 1/100th of a pound sterling (the British currency). So just like in the US, it is the smallest unit of money.

However, in British English, the word has two plural forms, each used in a specific situation:

  • Pennies — used when you are talking about the physical coins themselves.
    Example: "I found three pennies on the floor." (Three actual coins.)
  • Pence — used when you are talking about an amount of money.
    Example: "This sweet costs 50 pence." (A price, not individual coins.)

So you would say "I have two pennies in my pocket" (two coins), but "That costs two pence" (a monetary value of 2p). This distinction is unique to British English and does not apply in American English, where "pennies" is always the plural.
How Small Is a Penny, Really?

A penny represents such a tiny amount of money that in everyday modern life, it is often treated as nearly worthless. In the US, many stores now round prices to the nearest five cents to avoid dealing with pennies altogether. In fact, Canada abolished its penny in 2013 — they stopped making and distributing them because it cost more to produce a penny than the coin was actually worth.

This real-world irrelevance of the penny is important context for understanding the figurative uses of the word below.

Beyond its literal meaning as a coin, "penny" is used in English to mean a very tiny or trivial amount of money in general.

  • "I don't have a penny to my name." — This means the person has absolutely no money at all.
  • "Every penny counts." — Even the smallest amounts of money matter.

Because the penny is such a culturally familiar and symbolically "small" coin, English is full of expressions built around it. Understanding these will help you recognize the word in context far beyond its literal meaning.

"A penny for your thoughts"
Said to someone who seems lost in thought and quiet. You're playfully offering them one penny — i.e., almost nothing — in exchange for knowing what's on their mind. It's a gentle, casual way to ask, "What are you thinking about?"

"The penny dropped" (mainly British)
This means someone finally understood something that they had been confused about. The image is of an old coin-operated machine: you drop a penny in, and it finally starts working. When "the penny drops," the moment of understanding has arrived.
Example: "He was confused for a while, but then the penny dropped and he laughed."

"A pretty penny"
This means a large amount of money — the exact opposite of what you might expect! Despite "penny" suggesting smallness, this phrase means something was expensive.
Example: "That vacation must have cost them a pretty penny."

"Penny-pinching"
To be a penny-pincher (noun) or to penny-pinch (verb) means to be very stingy or overly careful with money — reluctant to spend even tiny amounts.
Example: "He's such a penny-pincher that he won't even buy a cup of coffee."

"Penny-wise, pound-foolish"
This is a proverb meaning someone is careful about small expenses but careless or wasteful about large expenses. A person who, say, obsesses over saving a few rupees on groceries but then wastes thousands on something impulsive would be called penny-wise and pound-foolish.

"In for a penny, in for a pound"
Once you've committed to something — even just a little — you might as well go all the way. If you've already taken a small risk, you may as well take the bigger one too.
Example: "I've already told her half the secret — in for a penny, in for a pound, I suppose."

"Turn up like a bad penny"
Said about a person or thing that is unwanted but keeps returning or reappearing unexpectedly.
Example: "He left the company but keeps turning up like a bad penny at every meeting."

"A penny saved is a penny earned"
A well-known proverb meaning that saving money is just as valuable as making money. If you avoid spending a penny, it's the same as having earned that penny.

"Penny ante"
An adjective meaning trivial, small-time, or not worth serious attention.
Example: "Don't worry about his complaints — it's just penny-ante stuff."
(Originally from poker, where "ante" is the small amount bet before the game begins.)

"Not a red cent / not a penny"
Both mean absolutely no money at all. "Not a penny" is used for zero money in any context.

In the world of finance and investing, penny stocks refers to shares of small companies that trade at very low prices — typically under five dollars per share in the US. The term signals that these are cheap, often risky, low-value investments. You'll encounter this term in business news.
A Quick Summary of What to Remember

• A penny is the smallest coin in a currency — worth one cent in the US/Canada, and one hundredth of a pound in the UK.
  • In British English, pennies = physical coins; pence = an amount of money.
  • Figuratively, "penny" suggests something tiny, trivial, or of minimal value.
  • The exception is "a pretty penny," which paradoxically means a large amount of money.
  • Phrases like "the penny dropped," "penny-pincher," and "a penny for your thoughts" are extremely common in everyday English conversation and writing.
